import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression


#### MISSING VALUES ####

# 1. Load the data from last week
df = pd.read_csv("data_updated.csv")

# 2. Add missing values in random rows
df.loc[np.random.choice(df.index, 5, replace=False), "age"] = np.nan
df.loc[np.random.choice(df.index, 2, replace=False), "iq"] = np.nan

# 3. Count missing values
print(df[["age", "iq"]].isna().sum())


#### DESCRIPTIVE STATISTICS ####

# 1. Age statistics (pandas ignores missing values by default)
print("mean:", df["age"].mean())
print("sd:", df["age"].std())
print("median:", df["age"].median())
print("min:", df["age"].min())
print("max:", df["age"].max())


#### LINEAR REGRESSION ####

# 1. Remove rows with NA in age or iq
df_clean = df.dropna(subset=["age", "iq"])

# 2. Unstandardized regression: age predicts iq
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(df_clean[["age"]], df_clean["iq"])
intercept = model.intercept_
slope = model.coef_[0]
print("intercept:", intercept, "slope:", slope)

# 3. Pearson correlation
print("Pearson r:", df_clean["age"].corr(df_clean["iq"]))


#### PLOT ####

# 1. Scatter plot of age and iq, axes cover the full range of each variable
plt.scatter(df_clean["age"], df_clean["iq"])
plt.xlim(df_clean["age"].min(), df_clean["age"].max())
plt.ylim(df_clean["iq"].min(), df_clean["iq"].max())
plt.title("IQ by age")
plt.xlabel("Age (years)")
plt.ylabel("IQ")

# 2. Regression line added manually from the coefficients
x_line = np.array([df_clean["age"].min(), df_clean["age"].max()])
plt.plot(x_line, intercept + slope * x_line, color="red")
plt.show()

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


#### CREATE VECTORS AND MATRIX ####

# 1. Sample two vectors
x1 = np.random.normal(loc=50, scale=10, size=15)
x2 = np.random.uniform(low=0, high=100, size=15)

# 2. Combine them into a matrix (each vector is a column)
x = np.column_stack((x1, x2))
print(x)


#### ARITHMETIC OPERATIONS ####

# 1. Scalar operations on x1
print(x1 + 5)
print(x1 - 5)
print(x1 * 5)
print(x1 / 5)

# 2. A second matrix of the same size, and matrix operations
y = np.column_stack((x1 + 2, x2 * 0.5))

print(x + y)
print(x - y)
print(x * y)     # element-wise multiplication


#### ACCESS AND MODIFY ELEMENTS ####
# Python counts from 0, so row 4 / column 2 is [3, 1]

# 1. Print and change the value in row 4, column 2
print(x[3, 1])
x[3, 1] = 33
print(x)

# 2. Extract row 5 and column 1 of the second matrix
row5 = y[4, :]
col1 = y[:, 0]
print(row5)
print(col1)


#### STATISTICS WITH MATRICES ####

# 1. Means and sums of rows (axis=1) and columns (axis=0)
print(x.mean(axis=1))
print(x.sum(axis=1))
print(x.mean(axis=0))
print(x.sum(axis=0))

# 2. Bonus: sum of squared deviations from the mean, per column
ssd_col = ((x - x.mean(axis=0)) ** 2).sum(axis=0)
print(ssd_col)

# 3. Insert 4 missing values in random cells, then count them
cells = np.random.choice(x.size, 4, replace=False)
x.flat[cells] = np.nan
print(x)
print(np.isnan(x).sum())


#### CONVERT TO DATA FRAME ####

df = pd.DataFrame(x, columns=["x1", "x2"])
print(df)

# Foundations of programming for empirical science
# Week 7
# assignment by < First Name > < Last Name >, id < 123456789 >

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)


#### LOAD AND MERGE FILES ####

# 1. Read all subject files with a for loop and bind them into one data frame
#    (the csv files are in the folder "stroop_data", inside the working folder)
file_list = list.files(path = "stroop_data", pattern = ".csv", full.names = TRUE)

df = data.frame()
for (file in file_list) {
  df_temp = read.csv(file)
  df      = rbind(df, df_temp)
}

# 2. Number of subjects and number of conditions
n_subjects   = length(unique(df$subject))
n_conditions = length(unique(df$condition))
cat("Number of subjects:", n_subjects, "\n")
cat("Number of conditions:", n_conditions, "\n")

# 3. Number and percent of missing RTs
cat("Missing RTs:", sum(is.na(df$rt)), "\n")
cat("Percent missing RTs:", mean(is.na(df$rt)) * 100, "\n")

# 4. RT histograms for congruent and incongruent trials
ggplot(df, aes(x = rt)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~condition) +
  labs(title = "RT by condition", x = "RT (ms)", y = "Count")


#### OUTLIERS ####

# 1. A function that flags RTs above mean + 2 SD
flag_outliers = function(rt) {
  m   = mean(rt, na.rm = TRUE)
  s   = sd(rt, na.rm = TRUE)
  out = rt > m + 2 * s
  return(out)
}

# 2. Loop over subjects: flag each subject's RTs by his own mean and SD,
#    and append the flags to one long vector (rows are ordered by subject)
outlier_flags = c()
for (s in unique(df$subject)) {
  rt_subj       = df$rt[df$subject == s]
  outliers_subj = flag_outliers(rt_subj)
  outlier_flags = c(outlier_flags, outliers_subj)
}

df$outlier = outlier_flags


#### PRESENT DATA ####

# 1. Number of outliers per subject
df |>
  group_by(subject) |>
  summarise(n_outliers = sum(outlier, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  print(n = Inf)

# 2. RT histograms again, after removing the outliers
df_clean = df |>
  filter(outlier == FALSE)

ggplot(df_clean, aes(x = rt)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~condition) +
  labs(title = "RT by condition, outliers removed", x = "RT (ms)", y = "Count")

# Foundations of programming for empirical science
# Week 7
# assignment by < First Name > < Last Name >, id < 123456789 >

import os
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


#### LOAD AND MERGE FILES ####

# 1. Read all subject files with a for loop and concatenate them into one data frame
#    (the csv files are in the folder "stroop_data", inside the working folder)
folder_path = "stroop_data"
df_list = []
for file in sorted(os.listdir(folder_path)):
    if file.endswith(".csv"):
        df_temp = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(folder_path, file))
        df_list.append(df_temp)

df = pd.concat(df_list, ignore_index=True)

# 2. Number of subjects and number of conditions
print("Number of subjects:", df["subject"].nunique())
print("Number of conditions:", df["condition"].nunique())

# 3. Number and percent of missing RTs
print("Missing RTs:", df["rt"].isna().sum())
print("Percent missing RTs:", df["rt"].isna().mean() * 100)

# 4. RT histograms for congruent and incongruent trials
for condition in ["congruent", "incongruent"]:
    plt.figure()
    plt.hist(df[df["condition"] == condition]["rt"].dropna(), bins=30)
    plt.title(f"RT - {condition}")
    plt.xlabel("RT (ms)")
    plt.ylabel("Count")
    plt.show()


#### OUTLIERS ####

# 1. A function that flags RTs above mean + 2 SD
def flag_outliers(rt):
    m = rt.mean()
    s = rt.std()
    out = rt > m + 2 * s
    return out

# 2. Loop over subjects: flag each subject's RTs by his own mean and SD,
#    and append the flags to one long list (rows are ordered by subject)
outlier_flags = []
for s in df["subject"].unique():
    rt_subj = df[df["subject"] == s]["rt"]
    outliers_subj = flag_outliers(rt_subj)
    outlier_flags.extend(outliers_subj)

df["outlier"] = outlier_flags


#### PRESENT DATA ####

# 1. Number of outliers per subject
print(df.groupby("subject")["outlier"].sum())

# 2. RT histograms again, after removing the outliers
df_clean = df[df["outlier"] == False]

for condition in ["congruent", "incongruent"]:
    plt.figure()
    plt.hist(df_clean[df_clean["condition"] == condition]["rt"], bins=30)
    plt.title(f"RT - {condition}, outliers removed")
    plt.xlabel("RT (ms)")
    plt.ylabel("Count")
    plt.show()

# Foundations of programming for empirical science
# Week 8
# assignment by < First Name > < Last Name >, id < 123456789 >

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)


#### BASIC PLOTS ####

# 1. Load the Titanic data and keep passengers with a known age
df = read.csv("titanic.csv")
df = df |>
  filter(!is.na(Age))
df$Pclass = as.factor(df$Pclass)

# 2. Mean survival by class and sex, with standard errors
df_surv = df |>
  group_by(Pclass, Sex) |>
  summarise(
    mean_surv = mean(Survived),
    se_surv   = sd(Survived) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

plot1 = ggplot(df_surv, aes(x = Pclass, y = mean_surv, fill = Sex)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.9)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_surv - se_surv, ymax = mean_surv + se_surv),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), width = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "Survival by class and sex", x = "Class", y = "Survival rate (mean +- SE)")

# 3. Age by class and sex (boxplot)
plot2 = ggplot(df, aes(x = Pclass, y = Age, fill = Sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Age by class and sex", x = "Class", y = "Age")

# 4. Another plot: age by survival (violin)
plot3 = ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(Survived), y = Age, fill = Sex)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(title = "Age by survival and sex", x = "Survived (0 = no, 1 = yes)", y = "Age")

# 5. Annotation: arrow and text on the survival plot
plot1 = plot1 +
  annotate("text", x = 1.25, y = 0.7, label = "Most women in 1st\nclass survived") +
  annotate("segment", x = 1.1, xend = 0.8, y = 0.78, yend = 0.97,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")))


#### MULTI-PANEL FIGURE ####

# 1. Survival plot on top (full width), the two age plots below it

# 1. Load the data, remove missing values, describe

df = na.omit(df)

dim(df)
summary(df)
table(df$species)

# 2. Scatter plot of two continuous variables, colored by species
ggplot(df, aes(x = bill_depth_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Bill depth and flipper length by species",
       x = "Bill depth (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)")


#### KNN MODEL ####

# 1. Seed, 80/20 split, the two predictors apart from the target
set.seed(42)
n           = nrow(df)
train_index = sample(1:n, size = round(0.8 * n))

predictors = c("bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm")
x_train = df[train_index, predictors]
x_test  = df[-train_index, predictors]
y_train = df$species[train_index]
y_test  = df$species[-train_index]

# 2. Standardize by the mean and sd of the training set
# Why: KNN classifies by the distance between penguins. Without standardization,
# the variable with the larger spread dominates the distance: flipper length
# varies by tens of mm, bill depth only by a few mm, so bill depth hardly counts.
train_mean = colMeans(x_train)
train_sd   = apply(x_train, 2, sd)

x_train_s = scale(x_train, center = train_mean, scale = train_sd)
x_test_s  = scale(x_test,  center = train_mean, scale = train_sd)

# 3. Loop over K = 1..20: train, predict the test set, save the accuracy
k_values = 1:20
accuracy = rep(NA, length(k_values))

for (k in k_values) {
  pred        = knn(train = x_train_s, test = x_test_s, cl = y_train, k = k)
  accuracy[k] = mean(pred == y_test)
}

# 4. Plot accuracy by K, with the best K marked in red
best_k  = which.max(accuracy)          # if several K tie, which.max takes the smallest
results = data.frame(k = k_values, accuracy = accuracy)

ggplot(results, aes(x = k, y = accuracy)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(data = results[best_k, ], color = "red", size = 4) +
  labs(title = "KNN test accuracy by K",
       x = "K (number of neighbors)", y = "Accuracy")

# 5. Print the best K and its accuracy
cat("Best K:", best_k, "accuracy:", accuracy[best_k], "\n")


#### BONUS ####

# 1. The same loop without standardization
accuracy_raw = rep(NA, length(k_values))

for (k in k_values) {
  pred            = knn(train = x_train, test = x_test, cl = y_train, k = k)
  accuracy_raw[k] = mean(pred == y_test)
}

print(round(accuracy_raw, 3))
# The best accuracy is lower: without standardization the distance is almost only
# flipper length, so the model nearly ignores bill depth, which helps to separate
# the species.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier


#### EXPLORE DATA ####

# 1. Load the data, remove missing values, describe
df = pd.read_csv("penguins.csv")
df = df.dropna()

print(df.shape)
print(df.describe())
print(df["species"].value_counts())

# 2. Scatter plot of two continuous variables, colored by species
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="bill_depth_mm", y="flipper_length_mm", hue="species")
plt.title("Bill depth and flipper length by species")
plt.xlabel("Bill depth (mm)")
plt.ylabel("Flipper length (mm)")
plt.show()


#### KNN MODEL ####

# 1. Seed (random_state), 80/20 split, the two predictors apart from the target
df_train, df_test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

predictors = ["bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm"]
x_train = df_train[predictors]
x_test  = df_test[predictors]
y_train = df_train["species"]
y_test  = df_test["species"]

# 2. Standardize by the mean and sd of the training set
# Why: KNN classifies by the distance between penguins. Without standardization,
# the variable with the larger spread dominates the distance: flipper length
# varies by tens of mm, bill depth only by a few mm, so bill depth hardly counts.
train_mean = x_train.mean()
train_sd   = x_train.std()

x_train_s = (x_train - train_mean) / train_sd
x_test_s  = (x_test - train_mean) / train_sd

# 3. Loop over K = 1..20: train, predict the test set, save the accuracy
k_values = list(range(1, 21))
accuracy = []

for k in k_values:
    model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)
    model.fit(x_train_s, y_train)
    accuracy.append(model.score(x_test_s, y_test))

# 4. Plot accuracy by K, with the best K marked in red
best_index = np.argmax(accuracy)        # if several K tie, argmax takes the smallest
best_k = k_values[best_index]

plt.plot(k_values, accuracy, marker="o")
plt.scatter(best_k, accuracy[best_index], color="red", s=120, zorder=3)
plt.title("KNN test accuracy by K")
plt.xlabel("K (number of neighbors)")
plt.ylabel("Accuracy")
plt.xticks(k_values)
plt.show()

# 5. Print the best K and its accuracy
print("Best K:", best_k, "accuracy:", accuracy[best_index])


#### BONUS ####

# 1. The same loop without standardization
accuracy_raw = []

for k in k_values:
    model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)
    model.fit(x_train, y_train)
    accuracy_raw.append(model.score(x_test, y_test))

print(np.round(accuracy_raw, 3))
# The best accuracy is lower: without standardization the distance is almost only
# flipper length, so the model nearly ignores bill depth, which helps to separate
# the species.

library(ggplot2)
library(class)
library(randomForest)


#### DATA PREPARATION ####

# 1. Load the data, dimensions, subjects per target value
df = read.csv("heart.csv")
dim(df)
table(df$target)

# 2. Remove duplicated patients: rows identical on all columns except bs
same_patient = duplicated(df[, c("age", "sex", "restbps", "chol", "maxhr", "target")])
sum(same_patient)
df = df[!same_patient, ]
nrow(df)

# 3. Data leakage: if the same patient is in both the training and the test set,
# the model is tested on subjects it has already seen (and can memorize). The
# test accuracy is then too optimistic and does not reflect new patients.

# 4. Seed and 70/30 split
set.seed(42)
n           = nrow(df)
train_index = sample(1:n, size = round(0.7 * n))

df_train = df[train_index, ]
df_test  = df[-train_index, ]

# 5. Standardize the predictors by the mean and sd of the training set only
# Why not the test set: the test set stands for new subjects the model has never
# seen. Using its mean and sd leaks information from the test set into the model,
# and makes the evaluation too optimistic.
predictors = c("age", "sex", "restbps", "chol", "bs", "maxhr")
train_mean = colMeans(df_train[, predictors])
train_sd   = apply(df_train[, predictors], 2, sd)

x_train = scale(df_train[, predictors], center = train_mean, scale = train_sd)
x_test  = scale(df_test[, predictors],  center = train_mean, scale = train_sd)
y_train = df_train$target
y_test  = df_test$target


#### THREE MODELS ####

# 1. Logistic regression: predicted probabilities for the test set
train_s     = data.frame(x_train, target = y_train)
logit_model = glm(target ~ ., data = train_s, family = binomial)
logit_prob  = predict(logit_model, newdata = data.frame(x_test), type = "response")
logit_class = ifelse(logit_prob >= 0.5, 1, 0)

# 2. KNN with K = 15: predicted class for the test set
knn_class = knn(train = x_train, test = x_test, cl = y_train, k = 15)
knn_class = as.numeric(as.character(knn_class))

# 3. Random forest with 500 trees: predicted probabilities and class
rf_model = randomForest(x = x_train, y = as.factor(y_train), ntree = 500)
rf_prob  = predict(rf_model, x_test, type = "prob")[, "1"]
rf_class = ifelse(rf_prob >= 0.5, 1, 0)


#### COMPARE PERFORMANCE ####

# 1. Confusion matrix for each model
table(Actual = y_test, Predicted = logit_class)
table(Actual = y_test, Predicted = knn_class)
table(Actual = y_test, Predicted = rf_class)

# 2. A function that returns accuracy, sensitivity and specificity
get_metrics = function(actual, predicted) {
  accuracy    = mean(predicted == actual)
  sensitivity = sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 1) / sum(actual == 1)
  specificity = sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 0) / sum(actual == 0)
  return(c(accuracy = accuracy, sensitivity = sensitivity, specificity = specificity))
}

# 3. One table: a row per model, a column per metric
results = data.frame(
  model = c("Logistic regression", "KNN (K = 15)", "Random forest"),
  rbind(get_metrics(y_test, logit_class),
        get_metrics(y_test, knn_class),
        get_metrics(y_test, rf_class))
)
print(results)

# 4. Bar plot of the accuracy of the three models
ggplot(results, aes(x = model, y = accuracy)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Test accuracy by model", x = "Model", y = "Accuracy")

# 5. Which model is better?
# After removing the duplicated patients the three models are close (about 0.7
# accuracy), and with only ~90 test patients the differences are small. Logistic
# regression is the simplest and about as good as the others, so I would prefer it.
# Before deciding we would want to know the cost of each error: missing a sick
# patient (low sensitivity) is usually worse than a false alarm, so we may prefer
# the model with the best sensitivity, or lower the 0.5 threshold. We would also
# check that the differences are stable across other splits of the data (see bonus).


#### BONUS ####

library(pROC)

# 1. AUC and ROC curves for logistic regression and random forest
roc_logit = roc(y_test, logit_prob)
roc_rf    = roc(y_test, rf_prob)
auc(roc_logit)
auc(roc_rf)

plot(roc_logit, col = "blue", legacy.axes = TRUE, main = "ROC curves - test set",
     xlab = "False Positive Rate", ylab = "True Positive Rate")
plot(roc_rf, col = "red", add = TRUE)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Logistic regression", "Random forest"),
       col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2)

# 2. Repeat the whole process with 5 seeds and average the accuracy
seeds    = 1:5
accuracy = data.frame()

for (s in seeds) {
  set.seed(s)
  train_index = sample(1:n, size = round(0.7 * n))
  df_train    = df[train_index, ]
  df_test     = df[-train_index, ]

  train_mean = colMeans(df_train[, predictors])
  train_sd   = apply(df_train[, predictors], 2, sd)
  x_train    = scale(df_train[, predictors], center = train_mean, scale = train_sd)
  x_test     = scale(df_test[, predictors],  center = train_mean, scale = train_sd)
  y_train    = df_train$target
  y_test     = df_test$target

  logit_model = glm(target ~ ., data = data.frame(x_train, target = y_train), family = binomial)
  logit_class = ifelse(predict(logit_model, data.frame(x_test), type = "response") >= 0.5, 1, 0)
  knn_class   = as.numeric(as.character(knn(x_train, x_test, cl = y_train, k = 15)))
  rf_model    = randomForest(x = x_train, y = as.factor(y_train), ntree = 500)
  rf_class    = ifelse(predict(rf_model, x_test, type = "prob")[, "1"] >= 0.5, 1, 0)

  accuracy = rbind(accuracy, data.frame(
    seed     = s,
    logistic = mean(logit_class == y_test),
    knn      = mean(knn_class == y_test),
    rf       = mean(rf_class == y_test)
  ))
}

print(accuracy)
colMeans(accuracy[, c("logistic", "knn", "rf")])
# The accuracy of each model changes by several points from seed to seed, and so
# does the ranking of the models. One split of ~300 patients is not enough to pick
# a winner; the average over seeds is more trustworthy (logistic regression is
# slightly ahead), but the models are close.

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, roc_curve, roc_auc_score

# the model is tested on subjects it has already seen (and can memorize). The
# test accuracy is then too optimistic and does not reflect new patients.

# 4. Seed (random_state) and 70/30 split
df_train, df_test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

# 5. Standardize the predictors by the mean and sd of the training set only

predictors = ["age", "sex", "restbps", "chol", "bs", "maxhr"]
train_mean = df_train[predictors].mean()
train_sd   = df_train[predictors].std()

x_train = (df_train[predictors] - train_mean) / train_sd
x_test  = (df_test[predictors] - train_mean) / train_sd

y_test  = df_test["target"]

print(confusion_matrix(y_test, knn_class))

    predicted = np.array(predicted)

     get_metrics(y_test, knn_class),

)

# regression is the simplest and about as good as the others, so I would prefer it.

# check that the differences are stable across other splits of the data (see bonus).


#### BONUS ####

# 1. AUC and ROC curves for logistic regression and random forest
print("AUC logistic:", roc_auc_score(y_test, logit_prob))
print("AUC random forest:", roc_auc_score(y_test, rf_prob))

fpr_rf, tpr_rf, _ = roc_curve(y_test, rf_prob)
plt.plot(fpr_logit, tpr_logit, label="Logistic regression")
plt.plot(fpr_rf, tpr_rf, label="Random forest")
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="gray")
plt.title("ROC curves - test set")
plt.xlabel("False Positive Rate")
plt.ylabel("True Positive Rate")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

# 2. Repeat the whole process with 5 seeds and average the accuracy
rows = []
for seed in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
    df_train, df_test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.3, random_state=seed)
    train_mean = df_train[predictors].mean()
    train_sd   = df_train[predictors].std()
    x_train = (df_train[predictors] - train_mean) / train_sd
    x_test  = (df_test[predictors] - train_mean) / train_sd
    y_train = df_train["target"]
    y_test  = df_test["target"]

    logit_model = LogisticRegression().fit(x_train, y_train)
    knn_model   = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15).fit(x_train, y_train)
    rf_model    = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=seed).fit(x_train, y_train)

    rows.append({
        "seed": seed,
        "logistic": logit_model.score(x_test, y_test),
        "knn": knn_model.score(x_test, y_test),
        "rf": rf_model.score(x_test, y_test)
    })

accuracy = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(accuracy)
print(accuracy[["logistic", "knn", "rf"]].mean())
# The accuracy of each model changes by several points from seed to seed, and so
# does the ranking of the models. One split of ~300 patients is not enough to pick
# a winner; the average over seeds is more trustworthy (logistic regression is
# slightly ahead), but the models are close.
